name: The Little Prince
blurb: Saint-Exupéry's fable of a stranded pilot and a boy who has traveled from a tiny asteroid
title: The Little Prince Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: The Little Prince summary: the pilot, the prince, the rose and the fox, the six planets in order, what happens at the end with the snake and what it means.
h1: The Little Prince: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: The Little Prince (Le Petit Prince) is a short illustrated book by the French writer and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, first published in New York in 1943 and in France in 1945. A pilot whose plane has broken down in the Sahara meets a small boy who says he comes from an asteroid. Over the days the pilot spends repairing his engine, the boy tells him about the flower he left behind and the strange adults he met on his travels. Written in simple language and read by children, it is also a book about friendship, loss and the way grown-ups lose sight of what matters.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: An aviator stranded in the Sahara after engine failure, who gave up drawing as a child
A boy with golden hair who lives alone on a tiny asteroid
A proud, beautiful flower that grows on the prince's asteroid
An animal the prince meets on Earth, who asks to be tamed
A yellow snake in the desert that speaks in riddles
The king, the conceited man, the drunkard, the businessman, the lamplighter, the geographer
The lone adults living on the six asteroids the prince visits before Earth

body: The narrator begins with a childhood memory. At six he drew a boa constrictor that had swallowed an elephant, but every adult who saw it thought it was a hat, so he gave up art and became a pilot. Years later his plane breaks down in the Sahara, a thousand miles from anywhere, with about a week of drinking water. At dawn a small boy wakes him and asks him to draw a sheep. The narrator's attempts are rejected until he draws a box and says the sheep is inside, which delights the boy. The boy recognizes the boa drawing at once.

Bit by bit the narrator learns the boy's story. The prince lives on asteroid B-612, a planet barely larger than a house, with three tiny volcanoes that he sweeps out and baobab seedlings that he must pull up every day before their roots can split the planet apart. One day a rose sprouted there. She was beautiful but vain and demanding, and her small lies made the prince doubt her love. He decided to leave, and only at the moment of goodbye did she admit she loved him.

The prince visited six asteroids, each with one adult. A king claims to rule everything but gives only orders that would happen anyway. A conceited man wants only to be admired. A drunkard drinks to forget that he is ashamed of drinking. A businessman counts the stars and believes he owns them. A lamplighter lights and puts out his single lamp once a minute, because his planet now turns that fast and his orders have never changed; the prince sees him as the only one who cares about something beyond himself. A geographer records mountains and rivers but never explores, and calls flowers ephemeral, which makes the prince worry about his rose for the first time. The geographer recommends Earth.

On Earth the prince lands in the African desert and meets a snake, who says he can send anyone back to where they came from. He finds a garden of five thousand roses that look exactly like his, and he weeps, thinking his rose was not special after all. Then a fox asks him to tame it, explaining that taming means building ties, so that two beings become unique to each other. When they part, the fox tells him that his rose is unique because of the time he has spent on her, and that the most important things cannot be seen with the eyes, only with the heart. The prince also meets a railway switchman who sends trains of hurried passengers back and forth, and a merchant selling pills that remove thirst and save time.
On the eighth day after the crash the narrator's water is gone. The prince suggests they look for a well, and after walking all night they find one at daybreak, and the narrator draws water for him.

The prince reveals that it has been a year since he arrived on Earth and that his star will be directly above the place he landed. He has arranged to meet the snake. The narrator, his engine finally repaired, finds him talking to it by a ruined wall. That night the prince tells him not to watch, saying his body is too heavy to carry home and will look like an empty shell. The snake bites his ankle, and he falls gently onto the sand without a sound. In the morning the body is gone.

The narrator flies home. Years later he believes the prince reached his planet, because no body was found, but he worries that he forgot to draw a strap for the sheep's muzzle and that it may eat the rose. The last page shows an empty desert landscape, and the narrator asks readers who find themselves there and meet a golden-haired boy to write and tell him.

Whether the prince dies or truly goes home is left open, and both readings are common. Taken literally, the snakebite is a death, and the book is about grief and how the people we love stay with us after we lose them. Taken as the prince and the narrator believe, the body is a shell he leaves behind to return to his rose, so the ending is about loyalty and responsibility. Many readers also connect the ending with Saint-Exupéry himself, who disappeared on a reconnaissance flight over the Mediterranean in July 1944, a year after the book appeared; that link is made by readers and biographers, not by the book.

ul: Children versus grown-ups: the adults on the six asteroids are absorbed in power, vanity, numbers or habit and miss what matters.
Love and responsibility: the fox teaches that taming creates ties, and the prince becomes responsible for his rose.
Seeing with the heart: the boa drawing, the box with the sheep and the hidden well all show that the essential is invisible.
Loss and grief: the narrator's friendship with the prince ends in separation, and the book is his way of remembering him.
Length: 27 short chapters, around 100 pages, with Saint-Exupéry's own watercolor illustrations, which are part of the story.
Original language: French; it has been translated into hundreds of languages and dialects.
Adaptations: many stage, radio, opera and ballet versions, a 1974 musical film, and a 2015 animated film directed by Mark Osborne.
Content advisory: the ending involves the implied death of a child, which can upset young readers.
What teachers usually ask about: what each asteroid adult represents, the fox's lesson about taming, and what the snake does at the end.

check.q: What does the narrator finally draw that satisfies the prince's request for a sheep?
options: A box with the sheep inside it
check.why: After several rejected drawings, the narrator draws a box and says the sheep is inside, and the prince is delighted.

check.q: What does the fox teach the prince?
options: That time spent on someone makes them unique to you
That all roses are the same
How to fix the pilot's plane
check.why: The fox explains taming: ties make a being unique, which is why the prince's rose matters to him.

check.q: How does the prince leave Earth at the end?
options: He climbs a mountain toward his star
He lets the snake bite him
check.why: The prince arranges for the snake to bite him, and his body has vanished the next morning.

faq.q: Does the Little Prince die at the end?
faq.a: The book leaves it open. The snake's bite reads as a death, but the body disappears and the narrator chooses to believe the prince returned to his planet.

faq.q: What does the rose represent in The Little Prince?
faq.a: The rose stands for a person the prince loves despite her flaws; many readers link her to Saint-Exupéry's wife, Consuelo, though the book itself does not say so.
It is the prince's home, a tiny planet with three small volcanoes, baobab seedlings that must be pulled up daily, and his rose.
